nameStory: The meadow evening primrose gets its name from its preferred habitat in open meadows and grasslands, combined with the evening primrose family's famous habit of opening their flowers in the evening hours. While this particular species actually blooms during the day, it shares the family name that comes from its night-blooming cousins who unfurl their petals as the sun sets.
description: Meadow evening primrose is a cheerful wildflower that produces bright yellow, four-petaled flowers in late spring and early summer. This native North American plant grows as a low-growing perennial herb, typically reaching 1-2 feet tall. It's sometimes grown in gardens for its sunny blooms and easy-care nature, making it a delightful addition to wildflower meadows and naturalized areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with exactly four rounded petals that feel silky-smooth to the touch, arranged in a simple cross pattern with eight prominent stamens in the center

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves with soft, fuzzy surfaces that feel slightly rough due to tiny hairs covering both sides

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing perennial that forms small clumps or patches, staying close to the ground with flowering stems rising 1-2 feet high

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, elongated seed capsules that split open when ripe to release tiny seeds with a slightly papery rattle when shaken

habitat: Look for meadow evening primrose in open grasslands, prairie remnants, and sunny meadows throughout New England, though it's quite uncommon with only 22 recorded observations in the region. It prefers well-drained soils in full sun locations and may occasionally appear in disturbed areas like roadsides or field edges.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of fuzzy leaves close to the ground, with flower buds beginning to form on emerging stems by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flowers opening during the day from late spring through early summer, followed by seed capsule development.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open to release seeds, while leaves may begin to yellow and die back in preparation for winter.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, with the plant surviving as underground roots ready to sprout again in spring.

funFact: Despite being called an "evening primrose," meadow evening primrose actually opens its flowers during the day, making it the rebel of its family since most of its relatives are famous for their romantic evening bloom shows that attract night-flying moths!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other yellow, four-petaled flowers like wild mustards, but evening primroses always have exactly eight stamens (the pollen-bearing parts) while mustards have six. Remember: "Eight for evening primrose, six for mustard tricks."
contextualKnowledge: The evening primrose family name can be confusing since several species in the group, including meadow evening primrose, actually bloom during daylight hours rather than in the evening. The family name stuck because the most well-known species are indeed evening bloomers.
compareHints: Meadow evening primrose is much less common than its cousin common evening primrose, which grows much taller (3-6 feet) and has larger flowers that open in the evening. Small sundrops are similar in size but have more deeply cup-shaped flowers, while meadow evening primrose has flatter, more open blooms that face upward toward the sun.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common evening-primrose is the tallest and most robust of New England's evening-primroses, with the largest flowers.
Small sundrops differs from its evening primrose relatives by staying low and sprawling rather than growing tall and upright like common evening primrose.
Among New England's evening primroses, northern evening primrose stands out for its smaller flower size compared to common evening primrose and Large-flowered evening-primrose.
Unlike the bold, large yellow flowers of common evening-primrose that can be 2 inches across, clockweed has tiny, delicate white or pink flowers only half an inch wide.
Unlike its yellow-flowered cousin common evening-primrose which grows tall and upright, pinkladies stays low and spreads horizontally.
Unlike its evening primrose cousins that typically have four-petaled yellow flowers opening at dusk, biennial beeblossom stands out with its pink flowers and incredibly tall, airy growth habit.
Unlike the tall, upright common evening primrose with its simple oval leaves, cutleaf evening primrose stays low to the ground with deeply divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Large-flowered evening primrose stands out from other Oenothera species primarily due to its impressive flower size - much larger than common evening primrose or the various sundrops species.
Among the many evening primroses in New England, red-stalked evening primrose stands out primarily for its reddish stem coloration, while most relatives like common evening primrose have green stems.
Unlike the common evening primrose which typically grows 3-5 feet tall, tall evening primrose can reach 6 feet, making it the giant of the genus.
Bigfruit evening primrose stands out dramatically from its New England relatives like common evening primrose due to its sprawling, ground-hugging growth habit rather than upright stems.
Yellow sundrops differ from common evening-primrose by blooming during the day rather than evening and having distinctive blue-green waxy leaves instead of plain green ones.
Among the evening-primroses in New England, Nodding Evening-Primrose is unique for its drooping flower buds - all other species have upright, erect buds.
